open_questions: Centroid on-target could not be tested (centroid_all not_run), but depth variability and grazing EB morphology already positively favor a binary on the target rather than a background blend, with no neighbour within 1 pixel able to plausibly cause it.
dossier.public_summary: TESS shows a 976 ppm dip that changes wildly between sectors and between individual transits, with a grazing V-shape and a large second dip at about 0.63 orbit. The transit depth is not stable and the grazingEB shape with secondary indicates a stellar eclipse on the target, not a planet.

reasons.why: Depth is not constant: 541 ppm in sector 2, 1580 ppm in sector 42, 23 ppm in sector 96. A real transit must have one depth; this changes dramatically.
Even within one light-curve product (SPOC 2-min) depth changes from 541 ppm to 1580 ppm (p_constant 6.513421733015099e-07) and QLP shows 23 ppm. Not a calibration offset, so not a planet.
Individual transits are highly inconsistent and dominated by a few outliers (e.g. 1683 ppm, 1482 ppm, 23 ppm, 374 ppm). A true planet dip repeats with the same depth.

A second dip in the same sector at ~0.63 orbit reaches 7.19 sigma and is about 21% the transit depth, well above the brightening check (5.501). Flat-bottom transit with a secondary at this depth points to a stellar companion, not a planet.
Ingress fraction 0.45 and a strong V (3.671 sigma) for a grazing geometry; fit impact parameter 0.9854 shows the dip is grazing, consistent with an EB and inconsistent with a Neptune-sized planet.
Independent scorer trained on vetted planets rates this as only 0.28 (below median planet 0.5 and far below secure planets), supporting a false-alarm interpretation over a planet.
